verbs.label: Contractility
verbs.info: Right ventricular contractility (Frank–Starling).

verbs.label: Tricuspid regurgitation
verbs.info: Systolic backflow into the right atrium: large v-waves reach the liver.

verbs.label: Pericardial constraint
verbs.info: Constrictive pericarditis limits filling.

verbs.label: Pregnancy
verbs.info: Weeks of pregnancy. Blood volume and cardiac output rise from the first trimester, and splanchnic vasodilation raises portal inflow, so portal pressure rises and varices enlarge. After 20 weeks the gravid uterus also raises the intra-abdominal pressure. 0 is before pregnancy.

verbs.label: Splenic vein thrombosis
verbs.info: Sinistral (left-sided) portal hypertension: splenic outflow decompresses through the short gastric veins.

verbs.label: Fibrosis · portal tract
verbs.info: Resistance before the sinusoids, as in schistosomiasis: portal pressure rises, the WHVP does not.

verbs.label: Fibrosis · portal tract
verbs.info: Resistance before the sinusoids, as in schistosomiasis: portal pressure rises, the WHVP does not.

verbs.label: Fibrosis · sinusoids
verbs.info: Collagen in the space of Disse and closing fenestrae: resistance in the sinusoids themselves, measured by the HVPG.

verbs.label: Fibrosis · sinusoids
verbs.info: Collagen in the space of Disse and closing fenestrae: resistance in the sinusoids themselves, measured by the HVPG.

verbs.label: Fibrosis · central vein
verbs.info: Resistance at the central veins, as in sinusoidal obstruction syndrome: the sinusoids congest from the outflow side.

lines: Blood enters the lobule here: portal venous blood (about three quarters) and hepatic arterial blood, with a bile ductule carrying bile the other way. Inlet venules run along the lobule’s edge and feed the sinusoids.
A branch of the portal venule running along the lobule’s border, feeding the sinusoids it passes.

A leaky capillary lined by fenestrated endothelium, between plates of hepatocytes one cell thick. Sinusoids merge toward the central vein, so blood speeds up as it goes; the highlighted path runs to the central vein.
A cross-link between sinusoids: blood can go around a local resistance, so one narrowed sinusoid does not leave the hepatocytes beyond it ischemic.
Collects the sinusoids and drains into the hepatic veins. Zone 3 around it gets the least oxygen.
Oxygen-rich blood that empties into the first stretch of the sinusoids (zone 1).
Bile made by hepatocytes flows in canaliculi between them, toward the triad: against the blood. Not part of the circulation, but it marks the portal tract.

Hepatocytes secrete bile into canaliculi, channels between neighboring hepatocytes sealed by tight junctions. Bile flows outward toward the portal tract, against the blood, and enters a canal of Hering at the limiting plate.

The canal of Hering joins the canaliculi to the bile ductule of the portal tract. It is lined partly by hepatocytes and partly by cholangiocytes, and harbors the progenitor cells that give rise to the ductular reaction in chronic liver injury.

Lymph is plasma that leaks from the sinusoids into the space of Disse, drains out through the tissue to the portal tract and leaves the liver in its lymphatics. It carries the protein that escapes the sinusoids, and returns the fluid to the blood through the thoracic duct.
Bands of collagen laid down by activated stellate cells bridge triad to triad and triad to central vein, cutting the lobules into regenerative nodules and distorting the vessels.
Zone 1 (periportal) gets blood first, richest in oxygen and nutrients: the first to regenerate, the last to undergo necrosis in ischemia.
Zone 2 lies between: intermediate oxygen.
Zone 3 (centrilobular) gets blood last, poorest in oxygen: first injured in congestion, shock and drug toxicity (acetaminophen).
